title: LEGO-PROVER: NEURAL THEOREM PROVING WITH GROWING LIBRARIES
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of neural theorem proving, specifically the difficulty large language models (LLMs) face when trying to prove formal mathematical theorems, including some at the middle-school level. The authors argue that existing approaches are limited by using a fixed theorem library during proving, which prevents reuse of useful lemmas across problems and makes long-chain proofs especially difficult.

To address this, they introduce LEGO-Prover, a system that uses ChatGPT as the LLM and combines a prover with an evolver around a growing skill library. The prover decomposes a theorem into subgoals, retrieves relevant verified lemmas from the library, and constructs proofs in a modular block-by-block fashion. The evolver then generalizes or solves newly proposed requests to create additional reusable skills, which are verified in Isabelle and added back to the library. The evaluation is conducted on the miniF2F benchmark, which consists of high-school mathematics competition problems formalized in Isabelle; the system is not an educational intervention with human learners.

The paper reports that LEGO-Prover improves pass rates on miniF2F compared with prior methods, reaching 57.0% on validation and 50.0% on test. The authors conclude that a growing library of verified lemmas can substantially improve theorem-proving performance and help bridge the gap between informal and formal mathematical reasoning.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is about neural theorem proving for formal mathematics, not an educational intervention study. It reports benchmark performance on miniF2F and ablations of an AI proof system, but there is no K-12 or student learning evaluation and no study design relevant to education evidence tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational impact on learners or schools. The reported gains are on theorem-proving pass rates in a formal mathematics benchmark (e.g., 57.0% vs 48.0%), which does not map to middle school mathematics achievement or classroom outcomes.
